summary: Describes an architecture for captive portals, the pages that networks use to make you log in or accept terms before using the network. The solution combines network provisioning protocols such as DHCP or Router Advertisements, an optional signaling protocol, and an HTTP API.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join coffee shop wifi and must click I agree first, that is a captive portal. This describes a tidy, standard way to build that.

questions: how does captive portal detection work
how does a device find the captive portal api
subtitle: How networks that demand a login or a click-through can tell devices about it without forging DNS or HTTP replies.

tldr.problem: Captive portals usually work by forging DNS or HTTP responses, which breaks protocols, confuses non-browser applications and defeats DNSSEC and TLS.
tldr.mechanism: The network hands the device the URI of a Captive Portal API through DHCP or Router Advertisements. The device queries that API over TLS for its captivity state and the User Portal URI, and an optional signal can hint that it should check again.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the components, the identifier a portal uses for a device and a sample workflow, but leaves the API details to other documents.

today: RFC 8952 is an Informational RFC published in November 2020 and has not been obsoleted or updated. The API it relies on is described in RFC 8908 and the provisioning option in RFC 8910.

sections.title: The Problem and the Requirements
sections.content:
A captive portal is a network that limits access until the user meets some conditions, such as reading advertisements, accepting an acceptable-use policy or providing credentials. Existing implementations typically forge DNS or HTTP responses, and some try to intercept HTTPS. Applications other than browsers are never told the network is captive.

The architecture is guided by these requirements:

  • Solutions MUST NOT require forging responses from DNS, HTTP or any other protocol.
  • They MUST let clients perform DNSSEC validation.
  • They MUST operate at the IP layer or above, not tied to Wi-Fi, cable or mobile.
  • Captivity SHOULD be explicitly available through a standard protocol.
  • They MUST provide a path of incremental migration.

The document focuses on devices with user interfaces and does not describe how devices without one could negotiate access.
sections.plainLanguage: Today the wifi often tricks your phone to show a sign-in page. This plan has the wifi simply tell your phone, so nothing is faked.

sections.title: The Components
sections.content:
The architecture has these parts:

  • User Equipment is the device, with a web browser, that wants full network access.
  • The Provisioning Service gives the device the Captive Portal API URI, using DHCP or Router Advertisements as in RFC 8910, or Provisioning Domains.
  • The Captive Portal API Server answers queries about the device's state of captivity.
  • The User Portal is the web server where the user satisfies the conditions.
  • The Enforcement Device blocks or allows traffic for each device and updates its rules when the User Portal directs it.

The Provisioning Service, API Server and User Portal are described as separate functions, but one entity might provide several of them.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a door guard, a front desk that tells you the rules, a sign-in page, and a note handed to you at the door saying where the front desk is.

sections.title: The API, the Signal and Device Duties
sections.content:
The API MUST support repeated queries from the same device and return the state of captivity. It MUST be able to give a URI for the User Portal, and that URI MUST use the https scheme. It MUST use TLS and be extensible. The details of the API are not specified here, but see RFC 8908.

The User Equipment MUST validate the API server's TLS certificate and MUST NOT call the API if validation fails. Most other device duties are SHOULDs, because users and legacy devices must not be forced to seek full access.

The optional Captive Portal Signal tells a device that its state may have changed. It carries no API URI, and all signals are treated as one hint to contact the API. The Enforcement Device MUST rate-limit signals, and devices SHOULD rate-limit API queries.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone checks the front desk over a safe connection. If the guard taps your shoulder, your phone just goes back and asks, but not too often.

sections.title: Identifying the Device
sections.content:
All components must agree on which device is which. A good identifier SHOULD uniquely identify the device, be hard to spoof, and be visible to both the API Server and the Enforcement Device.

The RFC evaluates three examples:

  • Physical interface is extremely hard to spoof, but only works if one device uses each interface, and the components must know about the interface.
  • IP address is unique at any time but can be spoofed, so solutions SHOULD try to prevent spoofing. With IPv6, identification could be done by subnet, such as the /64.
  • MAC address is often used today and may be used, subject to the same criteria.

URIs provided in the API SHOULD be unique to the device and not depend on context. Including unauthenticated identifiers in a URI may expose the service to spoofing or replay.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard and the front desk need a way to recognise you, like a name tag that is hard to fake and that both of them can read.

sections.title: A Sample Workflow
sections.content:
This section is not normative. On first connection, the device gets a DHCP lease or RA, learns the API URI, and queries the API in place of the clear-text canary request. If needed, the user visits the User Portal, which tells the Enforcement Device to allow the device. Access then lasts until conditions expire.

When expiry nears, the device compares its stored expiry time with the clock, checks the API again, and prompts the user to extend access through the User Portal. If the URI changes, for example on a DHCP renewal or a new RA, the device can fetch updated state at once or wait until the old conditions are about to expire.
sections.plainLanguage: You get a note on arrival, ask the front desk, sign in if needed, and later get a reminder to renew before your time runs out.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The network provides the portal URI, so it SHOULD do so securely, for example with the DHCPv6 AUTH option. Users who trust an attacking network might visit a malicious page and hand over credentials.

The API must be secured with TLS, since an attacker who captures its information could masquerade as the device, end its session or consume its quota. The signal only prompts a query, carries nothing that could mislead, and is rate-limited. Devices MAY let users turn off automatic reaction to signals for privacy, at the cost of not being notified.

A shared identifier could be abused to track the user, so identifiers should be stored securely and sent over encrypted channels such as TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trust the sign-in page if you trust the place. Keep your name tag private so nobody can follow you around.
